overview: This chapter follows Portuguese architecture and learning from the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries, through Lisbon's Belem complex and Coimbra's colleges, laboratories and printing facilities.

items.text: In sixteenth-century Belem, the Hieronymites monastery combined richly carved Manueline decoration with spaces for worship, meals, study and communal life.
The Belem tower incorporated ribbed cupolas inspired by Islamic architecture. Its design records artistic exchange across cultural boundaries.
Coimbra University has occupied the Royal Palace of Alcacova since 1537 and expanded through a network of colleges.
In the eighteenth century, Coimbra added chemistry and other laboratories, a botanical garden and a university press. These facilities linked teaching, experimentation and the circulation of books.
